title: Nightwatch
pitch: An incident console where the AI agent's tools mount as the incident gets worse and unregister when it is over. Escalation has to be argued for. The human on call holds the keys.
about_excerpt: An incident console where the AI agent's tools mount as the incident gets worse and unregister when it is over. Escalation has to be argued for. The human on call holds the keys. Like Comment Story Updates Console at green with the alert firing and charts spiked The escalation panel, "AGENT IS REQUESTING SEVERITY YELLOW" with its reason The approval card, frozen rollback call with Approve and Deny Charts curving back under the SLO after the approval Blue severity, the tray with destructive tools gone and 10 / 10 on the strip Inspiration Incident response is the job everyone wants to hand to an AI agent, and the job nobody actually dares to. It is three in the morning, the checkout service is failing, and the person on call is half awake. An agent could read the logs, compare the last deploy, and find the cause in seconds. But the fixes are dangerous. Rolling back the wrong thing or draining the wrong region at 3am makes a bad night much worse. So today you get two options, both bad. Give the agent standing access to the dangerous actions and carry that risk permanently, or give it nothing and do all the work yourself. WebMCP suggests a third option, because in WebMCP the tool surface belongs to the page, and the page can change it while the agent is mid conversation. That turns "what is this agent allowed to do" from a config file into live application state. We wanted to see what happens if an agent's permissions follow the incident instead of being fixed in advance, with a human deciding every step of the way. What it does Nightwatch is an incident console for a small group of production services. The left side is what the on call engineer sees: an alert, service health, live p99 and error rate charts against their SLO lines, and a timeline. The right side is what the agent sees: every tool it is currently allowed to call, and it changes with severity. At green, the agent gets four read only tools. It can see the service list, check health, read the console state, and ask for more access. Logs, deploy history, and anything that touches production do not exist for it yet. Not disabled. Not registered. At yellow, four investigation tools mount: the alert, logs, the last deploy's config diff, and the dependency graph. Still read only. At red, the tools that change production mount: rollback_deploy, drain_region, page_owner, and set_maintenance_mode. Every one of them freezes mid call on an approval card in the page until the human clicks Approve or Deny. The agent cannot click it. At blue, those four are unregistered and two postmortem tools take their place, so nobody can roll something back by accident an hour after it is over. Severity is human only. The agent has a request_escalation tool, but it never changes anything. It records the agent's evidence and lights up the button that only the person can press. In a typical run the agent is asked to look into checkout at green. It checks health, sees the breach, realises it has no logs, and asks for yellow with the numbers to justify it: 14.2% error rate against a 0.5% budget, 1840ms p99 against 300ms. You grant yellow. It reads the deploy diff and finds that the 03:04 deploy set the database connection pool to 4 instead of 400. You tell it to fix that. It asks for red, because the rollback tool does not exist yet. You grant red. It calls rollback, the approval card appears, and the whole call is held until you click. Deny it and it reports the system is still failing and stops. Approve it and the charts curve back under the SLO. Then you press blue, the four dangerous tools vanish, and the browser's own count drops from 14 to 10. Ask for the rollback again and the agent tells you the capability is gone and asks for red back. How we built it How we built it One HTML file, vanilla JavaScript, no build step, no backend. There are 14 tools, each declaring which severities it exists at. They are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool with a navigator.modelContext fallback, since the API moved to Document in the July draft and Chrome 150 deprecates the old location. The interesting part is the sync layer. It keeps one AbortController per tool. On every severity change it registers what has become permitted and aborts the signal for anything that has not. AbortSignal is the only unregistration path the spec has allowed since unregisterTool was removed on 23 April 2026. After each sync the page calls getTools() and shows the browser's count next to its own, so the tool surface is proved on screen rather than claimed. Read tools carry readOnlyHint. Destructive tools carry destructiveHint and block on a promise that only a DOM click resolves. We verified in ChatGPT's browser that a tool call can be held open for well over a minute waiting on that click without the agent timing out. The charts are a small simulation that follows checkout-api's live numbers: fast to spike, slow to recover, noisy while breaching. That is why the recovery after a rollback is a curve and not a step. The estate itself is synthetic. That is deliberate. Anyone opening the link at any hour gets the same incident, the same root cause, and the same fix. Wired to live telemetry there would be nothing wrong to investigate most of the time. What is not simulated is the WebMCP layer, and that is the part being demonstrated. Challenges we ran into We assumed ChatGPT's browser could unregister tools and built the first demo around it. Rather than trust that assumption we wrote probe.html, a page that walks the real modelContext object and reports what is actually there. It found five methods and no removal method at all. Re-registering an existing name threw. So we rebuilt around sealing: tools stayed registered and the page refused calls that were out of severity. It worked, and the reconciliation strip showed the gap honestly: 10 permitted, 4 sealed, 14 registered. Then we found that unregisterTool had not been left unimplemented, it had been replaced. Registration accepts an options object with an AbortSignal. We extended the probe, aborted a live signal, and getTools() confirmed the tool was gone. The seal came out and real unmounting went in. The probe stayed in the repo as the evidence trail. The second real challenge was narrative rather than technical. Our first version only started the incident when the human pressed yellow, which made the whole flow circular: you had to already know something was wrong to grant the agent access to find out. We moved the incident to fire on page load, so green is what it actually is on a real on call shift. An alert is firing, and nobody has triaged it yet. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent asks for permission on its own. Nothing in a prompt tells it to. It works out that it can't read logs, notices that request_escalation exists, and argues its case with the actual numbers off the console. live_observation.first_impression: Nightwatch presents an incident console with services, human-controlled severity buttons, a human-plus-agent timeline, and mounted/unmounted capabilities.
live_observation.after_state: The page visually remained unchanged: YELLOW was still available and the headings still reported four capabilities mounted; no escalation or approval card became visible.
live_observation.notes: The severity control is available, but the expected escalation state was not observable after one click.
